utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Radinovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The cross-examination by Mr. Stamp will now continue. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yesterday you referred to the collegium meeting in which the -- there was discussion about the 47.000 armed Serb civilians. In that meeting, Dusan Samardzic, who was the former commander of the 3rd Army, said -- and this is page 23. I don't know if you need to see it. I'm just going to read it. Because you indicated that you had gone through it before. "It was my order, and we organised the whole thing for the defence of Serbian villages. Commanders at all levels have been sent out. They're armed and they have two combat sets of ammunition each. Their role and assignment is to defend their villages and participate together with army units in any operation in the immediate vicinity. We have to carry out military and police operations. It can't be done in any other way. And at this moment, they are -- there are enough army and MUP members to do their part of the job, if it should come to that." General Samardzic seems to be speaking about arming Serb villagers, and you suggested yesterday that the 47.000 armed Serbs included MUP reservists, civil protection personnel, civil defence personnel, Territorial Defence personnel. Isn't that inconsistent with what the general said that he did?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not inconsistent with what the general said. I had in my hands a document - I think it was from May 1998 - this document orders the arming of civilians, but members of the reserve force of the Army of Yugoslavia and the military territorial units. So in that document, we can see that these are military conscripts who are being issued with weapons and equipment in case that proves to be impossible in a situation when there are war operations. Furthermore, you have documents of the Ministry of the Interior in which information is provided about members of the civil protection, civil defence, the system of reporting and monitoring, and the coding and communications units. All these categories, including reserve police units, are being armed as civilian population. So from civilian population, they turn into military conscripts. In addition to that, there is an order issued by the chief of the defence department of Pristina, Colonel Petar Ilic, in which he issues an order. Once there was this spontaneous self-organisation of the population, in order to prevent any mistakes in this process, he orders the chiefs of his military offices that the arming of the civilian population should be done in an organised fashion; namely, arms should be issued only to those who do not have wartime assignments in units of the military, in military territorial units, in units of the civil defence --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter can no longer hear the witness because of background noise from somebody's microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just -- just a moment, Mr. Radinovic. There's a problem with interpretation. Could you just go back a little in your answer there about two or three sentences and continue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I hope I get the right spot where it was that I was interrupted with this noise. This order issued by Colonel Ilic pertains to the arming of the civilian population outside the military deployment of the army of the units civil defence, civil protection units, the civil -- the system of reporting, and the coding and communications units of the Ministry of Defence. So it is only in this situation that we are dealing with the civilian population in the literal sense of the word. Now, these are facts that can be established on the basis of documents that the Prosecutor probably has, as well as the Defence, because I had them available to me when I was working on my report. What I'm going to say now is my own analysis and my own assessment. If we are talking about the non-Albanian population - and obviously we are - if we know that in Kosovo and Metohija at that time, at the time that we are discussing here, there were between 200 and 250 thousand non-Albanians; also, if world standards of maximum mobilisation rates of the population, bearing in mind the population of military-age population within the demographic population in general, the rate is between 10 to 12 per cent - and Germany was even up to 15 per cent - then this figure of 47.000 certainly could not pertain to armed civilian population in the literal sense of the word; that is to say, outside the wartime assignment of the units that I spoke about. Therefore, in my analysis, in my assessment, bearing in mind the personnel levels of the Pristina Corps, the personnel levels of the military territorial units, the units of the reserve police, and the forces of the Ministry of the Interior, including the civil protection and civil defence, the reporting system, and the coding system, I reached the figure of between 4 to 6 thousand at a maximum; that is to say, civilians who could be used as village guards and possibly in that context that we called "armed civilians." So this figure that I mentioned is on the basis of my own analysis. What I said earlier on is based on figures and facts only.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The figure of up to 15 per cent, 10, 12, or 15 per cent, is that a figure relating to formal mobilisation of the population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the overall demographic strain that a population can take, in terms of the army and mobilisation, and so on. If we take into account that there is a percentage of women, children, the elderly, and so on. So we are really talking about men who are of military age, between the ages of 18 and 60, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But it doesn't follow that that would be the percentage of the population who are male and between the age of 18 and 60, does it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid I don't understand what it is that you are asking me now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you give us a figure for the -- a rough figure for the percentage of the population that are male between the ages of 18 and 60?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that would be the percentage that I gave you, between 10 and 15 per cent of the population. That is the population that is able-bodied, military age. The 15 per cent of the 250.000 mentioned was supposed to man everything that I referred to. And as a matter of fact, these wartime units could not be manned only from Kosovo but quite a few had to be manned on an extraterritorial basis. I simply cannot accept this figure of 47.000 armed civilians without including military conscripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Forget arming just for the moment and just looking at the population as a whole, what percentage of the population, in general and rough terms, is male and between the ages of 18 and 60?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I already said; it's about 15 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Wouldn't the MUP be responsible to arm its own reservists or its own established structure?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, yes. The MUP was -- well, I'm -- I'm talking about the figure of 47.000. 47.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the figure that could not have been manned, so to speak, from the -- among the civilians who did not have a wartime assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. We've heard that now.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course this can be challenged, but quite frankly, this is my analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, I understand you to be saying that. What I'm asking you is about the MUP. You told us yesterday that the 47.000 would have included MUP reservists. And I think you're telling us now that the MUP would have been responsible to arm its own reservists or its own established system. Wouldn't the civilian protection and the civilian defence units be armed through their organisation in the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that had been discussed here already, but I'm going to repeat this. Weapons for the civil defence and civil protection units, for the reporting and observation units and the communications and coding units, is kept in military storage and military warehouses, depots, precisely earmarked that these are weapons that can be taken only at the request of the officers of those units, but it is stored and guarded in military facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What type of weapons would civil protection personnel be issued with?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only personal defence weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What type of weapons would civilian protection -- sorry, civilian defence personnel be issued with?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civilian defence personnel would be issued with sidearms, rifles, ordinary, semiautomatic, automatic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I think you said in your report - but you could just let me know without having to go there - that these would not be assigned -- ought not to be assigned combat tasks?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. Combat assignments would not be assigned. They are used for guarding facilities of special importance, in civilian terms; then for securing settlements; but not combat units. They can get assignments from battalion commanders in the field; however, only within that mandate. So in the sense of control, yes, the battalion commander can control them. The one carrying out combat tasks, combat activities at such-and-such a territory, but the task issued to them can only be within the mandate of civil defence units.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: General Samardzic, a former commander of the 3rd Army, in discussing his distribution of the weapons, said that they were armed with two sets of combat ammunition each. Their role and assignment is -- is to defend their villages and participate together with army units in any operations in the immediate vicinity. Why -- why would civilian defence units, civilian protection units, MUP reservist units, be issued with combat ammunition and task unestablishment with assisting -- with defending villages and assisting the army in operations?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was an internal war. It was an inter-ethnic war in which at every moment -- well, you know what it's like when you have settlements with a mixed population and when the non-Albanian population was a minority. It was very easy to have a pogrom of that population, and that did indeed happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was only natural to have settlements protected, defended from attacks by the Siptar terrorist forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At the -- could we have a look at P929, please. 928. Forgive me. This is the collegium minutes for the 28th of December. And I think you indicated that you had read these minutes. I'm afraid I can't find for you the page I'm going to read in English. I can't find the B/C/S corresponding page, but this is page 9 of the English. We have General Dimitrijevic saying, in respect to Kosovo and Metohija at this collegium: "I am thinking of a figure of about 60.000 armed Serbs that can be mobilised outside the control of -- of the official organs." And you -- you recall reading General Dimitrijevic saying that at the collegium?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall, but now I don't have the text in front of me, so I cannot see it exactly, but there is no reason for me not to believe you, because I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What -- well, who would have armed these 60.000 Serbs that he's speaking of?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I understood this, he did not say that they were actually armed but that they could be armed; whereas, I think that they could not be armed. I disagree with Dimitrijevic on that, because he didn't do his math right. But, okay, that is his opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. So your position is based on a -- a demographic assessment, I take it.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You saw some combat orders. I have a list of them, but to save time, perhaps I might need to show you - in which VJ units were ordered to engage in operations and to be reinforced and deployed with armed civilians. They refer to the armed -- armed non-Siptar population. You saw those orders or any orders of this nature? I just ask you in the interest of time, because I don't want to have to go through these orders. They have come before the Court many times.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but it's not the way you put it. That is not what is written there. It is not stated that it should be reinforced, because reinforcing units with armed non-Siptar population would imply that they were being added to units as combat personnel, and that is not contained anywhere in the orders issued by commanders, that these units are being issued tasks of combat units.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. My mistake. What I'm saying is that they there were orders in which VJ units would be mobilised or deployed for combat along with what was described as the armed non-Siptar population. You saw those orders, or shall we look at a couple of them?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not to go into combat with them. This armed non-Siptar population should carry out its tasks within its missions, and that is only the protection of facilities that are meant for general purposes, for civilian use, and to protect the population and settlements, not to carry out other combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We'll look at one them, and I represent to you that there are many in similar terms to this. Could I have a look at 20 -- P2015, page 2 -- well, we've -- page 1, just to identify it. This is an order of the 23rd of March, 1999 from the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija, strictly confidential number 455-63. If we could go to page 2 there. And I think I can see item 2 on top of your page, also at the top of the English page, and it speaks of Pristina Corps assignments, and it says: "With reinforcements and armed non-Siptar population from Kosovo and Metohija, the Pristina Corps is assisting the MUP in crushing and destroying STS in the zone of responsibility." This does refer to the armed non-Siptar population so-called protecting - what is it? - protecting civilian facilities, I think you said. This implies their -- their being involved in crushing.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So let me ask you this: When they were employed or engaged --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, no, they certainly would not be engaged in this destroying. Try to find the right pages and see whether they go out there to destroy. This formulation has a purpose of its own. It's not engagement yet. This is just an indication that there is armed non-Siptar population this the area of responsibility, and only when we see what their task is can we give comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mean, whether they're being used for the right purpose or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is the task not what's set out immediately afterwards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the task of the corps. Well, yes, yes, the task of the corps, but not of that population. Because the order issuing authority is probably going to order that population what it is that they're supposed to do. What I expect to see in paragraph 5 is what their task is going to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The question I was about to ask is this: If and when armed civilians are engaged or act along with VJ units, wouldn't the members or the -- the armed civilians be under the effective control of VJ commanders?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they are re-subordinated to him, yes. If they are not re-subordinated to him, then no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When armed civilians are re-subordinated -- all right. Let's not enter the re-subordination debate at this point in time. If armed civilians who are trained by the VJ and armed by the VJ are engaged in tasks in coordination of the VJ, to whom are these armed civilians responsible? What organisation is responsible for them?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When civilians are armed, regardless of whether they are conscripts or not, they become an integral part of the forces of the Ministry of the -- of Defence; that is to say, that when they receive weapons, they become part of the civilian defence, regardless of -- that is what they were envisaged as in terms of establishment in advance. They are commanded by the officer of the civil defence organ. If it's a unit, then the unit has its commanding officer, who is subordinated in the vertical chain of command. As for that, you have the order of General Manastirac [phoen], who was chief of the regional defence organ for Serbia and Pristina was subordinated to him, and his document -- I can't remember the exact number now, but I did quote it in his paper -- he says that he explicitly forbids civil defence unit commanders and members to respond to anybody's orders but those coming from the Ministry of Defence. That is explicit. And I assume that it is binding on civil defence units that were in the zone of this --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters could not hear the end of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm sorry. In any case, general, when we're talking about civil defence units now, we are talking about what you referred to as armed non-Siptar population as a distinct group from civil protection and civil defence, and I remind you -- if we could look at what you said yesterday. Just a minute. Yesterday at 17269, line 19 and thereafter, you said that this group of 47.000 armed civilians that General Samardzic mentioned at the collegium should be seen as including all the members of the reservists, army resist, the territorial units, the reserve forces units were mentioned, and the 47.000 units -- 47.000 also includes units of civil protection and civil defence and what is colloquially referred to as the armed non-Siptar population. So I don't want us to be speaking about all those other units that you claim make up the 47.000. I want to speak of -- we're talking about the armed non-Siptar population which is referred to in these orders, which were armed by the VJ. What organisation did they command when they were acting with the VJ?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that earlier. If we're talking about civilians who do not have a war assignment in the military or the police, then they belong to the Ministry of Defence forces, regardless of whether before they were in the establishment of the formations of the civilian defence and other forces, so they're always part of the Ministry of Defence. As soon as they get weapons, they become members of the civilian defence and are placed under the command of the system of command of the forces of the Ministry of Defence. This is what I wanted to say. This is what I meant to say yesterday, today. This is what I've always thought. But in order to answer this question of yours, can we please look at paragraph 5 of this document, where it should state what the units -- what the non-armed -- that the armed non-Siptar population's tasks are. That would be the simplest way of doing it to see which tasks they are given.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We could look at paragraph 5, but I could mention now that the armed Siptar star population are not mentioned -- is not mentioned there. But let us move to paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Sorry for the interruption. I apologise for this. Now, really the -- you have to kindly help us understand the ground realities, because what is happening in the fields at the war zone, at -- because the Ministry of Defence will not be having personnel or -- like the VJ or the commanders or somebody to control the forces on the ground. So where these people get inducted to do -- they cannot get every little order from the Ministry of Defence, because Ministry of Defence has a different role altogether. The bureaucracy there is very short. It's actually the field situation. Would you kindly help us in understanding what really happened on the -- in the field situation vis-a-vis these non- -- these armed non-Siptar population.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the defence ministry has its own command line. The ministry is at the top. Then there are sectors: The sector for civilian defence, the sector for the military economy. The sector for the civilian defence has sub-organs or regional organs for the Republic of Serbia and the Republic of Montenegro. In Serbia it has a sector for the province of Kosovo and Metohija and the province of Vojvodina. The administration -- defence administration of Pristina, which was the regional organ, in order to conduct the defence in the province of Kosovo, has its own regional organs in the depth. These would be sections, departments, defence secretariats, and so on. In all of the territory, each of those regional organs would be commanding the units of the defence ministry. It -- these are not large units. You've seen in the documents which were introduced through General Farkas when he testified here, these are numbers around 3.700 in the civilian protection and in the civilian defence, 3.800 something like that, then something in observation, and monitoring, a crypto-protection. So it's around 6.000, and this is deployed throughout the whole territory. These are small groups that are being used to guard villages, village guards, patrols in order to guard schools, hospitals, milk factories, bakeries. These facilities that are being used to supply the civilian population. These are the kind of assignments that they perform. They receive assignments from their superiors along the chain of command of the forces of the Ministry of Defence. When a military commander of a battalion of the army finds himself in that area where civilian defence unit is, he has the right to oversee it. He's authorised to monitor it, to see how it's performing its special task, but he cannot give them an assignment. So this is the simplest story that I could tell you, and I don't know if that is satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You did elucidate. But the question is: Why arm them, then? Because they were performing Social Services, like any other -- any other factor with respect to the civil defence: Fire extinction, hospitals, things like that. Why -- why arm them and what is then meant by "mobilisation"? I just need your help for that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because there was a very intense inter-ethnic conflict in Kosovo and Metohija underway in which civilians were also casualties and where the population was mixed. There was a mutual conflict, settling of accounts, revenge, facilities are destroyed, there are attempts at looting, seizure. And, of course, in those situations, those facilities are protected, and for that protection local population is usually used to patrol villages, to prevent the appearance of gangs or self-proclaimed soldiers, fighters. Anything can happen in the war, especially in mixed communities, and that is the experience in the wars in the territory of the former Yugoslavia from 1991 to 1999. That's why it was necessary for the civilian protection units. The civilian protection is an entirely different system. It's supposed to deal with the technical effects of natural disasters, floods, earthquakes, and other disasters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: In that case, shouldn't they be the part of MUP, or given over to MUP, because they were performing such duties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not an expert on the MUP, but MUP has a different mandate. It deals with security questions. It monitors and controls traffic, prevents crimes; it deals with problems of determining the identity of unknown persons; the tasks that are usually performed by any police in the world. Civilians are not trained for those kinds of tasks. This is something that has to be done by specials -- specialists or professionals who were trained for those sorts of tasks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry. You are suggesting the civil protection and civil defence groupings that are being described in part here as "spontaneously self-organising," these are the sort of specially trained people you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Your Honour, I was talking about -- I was asked by His Honour about assignments in the field, if they -- the protection of facilities should be carried out by police forces, and I said that policemen have to go through special training for those kinds of assignments. So perhaps I made a slip. This is what I meant. Units of the civilian protection and civilian defence I did not consider to be a spontaneous form of self-organisation of people for purposes of defence. What I meant was the armed population that did not belong to the civilian defence, the civilian protections, or other elements of the system. In the course of 1998, this spontaneous self-organising did occur, and in order to avoid the consequences of that self-organising, organs of the Ministry of Defence ordered that this should be done in an organised manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Judge Chowhan started that series of questions by asking you what the situation was like on the ground. I'm afraid I'm as ignorant now as I was before your answer started. Who actually commanded these people on the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you're thinking of armed non-Siptar population? Is that what you're thinking of?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The ones who chose to lift arms because of the situation, who commanded them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were under the command of the organs of the Ministry of Defence, the section of the Ministry of Defence in the territory where they were. In the field itself, there are the lowest command organs of the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I -- I still don't understand. Are you -- we are at -- you are at odds with -- with senior army officers who talk about possibly 47.000 or even 60.000 such people, but let -- even assuming your small number, which is part of the 6.000 that -- that you've given us, if -- if they decide the situation merits using the arms which apparently they have in their homes, how -- how are they organised for any particular task? Who commands them? How do they know who it is that -- that's in charge if they're the ones that have decided spontaneously to group together for the purpose of facing up to terrorist activity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document that I mentioned explicitly orders that while arming civilians, senior officers should be appointed, the senior officers of the village guards and the patrols, and they are executing immediate command. They have their superiors within the system of command of the Ministry of Defence. This is a system of control that begins -- that goes from the top to the down, just like there is the command system in the army from the top down. This exists in the MUP as well. These are three systems that are a whole. They go from the top to the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we look at P2015 again. And to save some time, you know, we don't need to go to 5 because 5 sets out tasks for the Pristina Corps, what they're supposed to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you don't go, I'll be going there, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Because the witness is telling us that the tasks for these civilians -- or civil defence or civil protection will be set out in paragraph 5. So we need to see what these tasks are.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, let's move to paragraph 5, but -- and that is on page 3 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What I want to ask you first is that where I read in paragraph 2 earlier the assignment of the Pristina Corps is given as being with reinforcements and armed non-Siptar population from Kosovo and Metohija, the PrK is assisting the MUP in crushing and destroying the STS in the zone of responsibility. And in paragraph 2 it also gives a task of the Pristina Corps. It would not be necessary to set out specific tasks for the armed non-Siptar population because a commander of the VJ over the rank of battalion, under Article 63 of the Law of Defence, is empowered to order the civilian -- the armed non-Siptar population to do special tasks.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid that you did not formulate that correctly or read it --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Formulate it. I will. I will.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Under Article 63 of the FRY Law on Defence, a battalion commander is empowered to assign a special task to armed members of the civilian population. And when they --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't say that. I -- I don't have the -- actually, I do have the law with me, and it does not say that definitely that the battalion commander would use civilians for special assignments. That definitely is not how it was. It would be best to see that article.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In Article 63 the guards patrolling the units of the special defence shall be commanded by state organs responsible for state defence ask protection. An officer of the Army of Yugoslavia who is in a position of battalion commander or higher may issue special tasks --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: "An officer of the Army of Yugoslavia holding a position of battalion commander or higher may issue special tasks concerning the defence and protection of the civilian population and material sources to units from paragraph 1 of this article and control them in the area of his responsibility." So would you agree with me that these units --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in order to avoid further discussions which I think will not lead us anywhere, P985, page 6 in B/C/S, should be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's a matter for Mr. Stamp how he conducts his cross-examination. Mr. Visnjic, you know you'll have your opportunity to re-examine if there's anything misleading occurs. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think there's been a confusion, because that article was not interpreted correctly to the witness, so at least if something is being quoted to him, it should be interpreted correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're saying something inaccurate occurred in the translation? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the interpreters do not have the document, so they are translating or interpreting on the basis of what Mr. Stamp is saying. But we're talking about a law. We have a double-translation of a -- an article from the law, and I think that would lead us to a situation that will take half an hour to clarify, so that is why I am saying that we should look at the original and then we continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sure that what Mr. Stamp has read is not stated in the article itself. I apologise. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We will come -- we will now come to that in a moment. Before we do, to avoid coming back to the document that's on the screen at the moment, Mr. Stamp, can we ask the witness to look through Article -- or paragraph 5 of this order and to identify for us where the tasks are allocated to the armed non-Siptar population. Could you do that, please. It may mean turning a page, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I see it. Article 5, where the assignments are issued to subordinate units, does not contain an item that would refer to the civilian population, which means that the commander organising the activities and is executing the order did not get those civilians as his subordinates and he's not obliged to issue assignments to them. They are working within their own mission, what they would usually be doing: Patrolling, protecting the village, facilities, what they would usually be doing. And then within those assignments, the battalion commander can tour the units and check if they are doing them properly. That's all. But he cannot change the actual assignment that they're doing. If the commander who drafted this order had believed that the armed group was subordinate to him, then he would have to issue it an assignment. Explicitly he would have to state their assignment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Stamp, if you're going to pursue the question of the Law on Defence, then I think we should have the Article 63 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you wish to complete this matter first, then please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, Witness, when the order provides for the task and assignment of the Pristina Corps simply with reinforcements and -- and armed non-Siptar population from the KiM, the Pristina Corps is assisting the MUP in crushing and destroying the STS in the zone of responsibility, I suggest to you it is not necessary to give specific tasks in a military document in paragraph 5 to civilian units because these units could be commanded by any officer of a VJ -- of the VJ over the rank of a battalion commander pursuant to Article 63 of the Law of Defence. That's the first -- the first part of the question, if I may -- may break it up: It would not be necessary or appropriate to give specific orders in paragraph 5 of a military document to civilian units. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. I assure you that any document of a command or an order, if you look at it - and I've seen thousands in this case - if you take an example and find any document which says "order of the commander for specific actions, attack, assault, march, defence," if he does not issue in Article 5 an assignment to each segment that is subordinated to the first degree, if you find something like that, then I -- I will strip my general's rank. This is the ABC of the profession. Any commander in the army knows that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Of civilian groups on the ground, the civilian groups on the ground are commanded -- this is the next question: Is it correct that pursuant to Article 63 of the Law on Defence civilian units on the ground can be given tasks by any commander from battalion commander up if they are in the zone of responsibility? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. That is not what it says in Article 63. It says something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: P985. And it's page 9 of the English. It's --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Wouldn't you agree with me, General, that at least when it came to --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the article. I don't have Article 63.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Perhaps counsel could have --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Page 6. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Wouldn't you agree with me - and that's all I'm asking - is that at least when it comes to the units of the civilian defence, that a VJ commander of battalion rank or higher may issue to them tasks once they are in the zone of responsibility under that law?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Literally it says here that it -- they can issue this but not that they always do that. And you also missed the part that follows, that an officer of the Army of Yugoslavia holding the position of battalion commander or higher may issue, from paragraph 1 of this article, special tasks concerning the defence and protection of the civilian population and material resources to units from -- and control them in the area of his responsibility but only in the sphere of these assignments, the assignments from the sphere of civilian protection and defence and material resources. They cannot be used for other types of assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp did in fact, certainly in English, accurately refer to these limitations. That may have been a difficulty in translation. I don't know. But he -- he didn't misrepresent the position to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So isn't it the situation that when an order, for example, from the corps commander is sent for operations in the field and the task of the Pristina Corps is to support the MUP, in association with the so-called armed non-Siptar population, then on the ground at battalion level where the operations are conducted the battalion commander, who has specific orders, may control these units and issue orders for special tasks to these units in the course of the operations on the ground at that level. So the order need not specifically task them, civilians, in paragraph 5. That is all I'm suggesting to you.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're not right on that. You are absolutely not right on that. If the superior officer - say, the commander of the Pristina Corps - dealt with one of his brigade commanders, giving him the task of controlling parts -- or rather, something that is called the unarmed non-Siptar population, then that commander is duty-bound to order that in his own order to his battalion commanders. That is quite certain. That's the way it is. It cannot be any other way. If he is given something, then what is given to him has to be used in the prescribed manner; meaning that if the Pristina Corps has this population under its control, then, according to -- then in paragraph 5 he has to be given the task that he has to carry out, and that is how the battalion commander can exercise control over that. That is what I've been saying all along.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for abuse, I'm not talking about that now. I'm talking about the system dealt with this. Units that are subordinated -- all units that are subordinated have to receive their tasks from their superior officer. That is the principle of subordination and singleness of command, and it is within that task that they are controlled.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's have a look quickly at -- at paragraph 76 of your report, page 27. That's part 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Radinovic, does that mean that to get the answer to whether any task was assigned by the VJ, the Army of Yugoslavia, to the armed non-Siptar population here, we would require to see an order from someone in the Ministry of Defence in the command structure of the armed non-Siptar population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as for this task, according to the system, one knows exactly what it is that they are doing. A patrol is not supposed to be given a task every time. They patrol a certain area, a certain street, a certain neighbourhood. They guard a facility or a bridge or a flyover or whatever. However, if they are being subordinated to the army, then the army has to order in paragraph 5 what it is that they are supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. So we don't need to see the order from the Ministry of Defence in relation to re-subordination. We can simply accept, according to you, that if there's nothing in Article 5 of the order, then they were not under the control of the Army of Yugoslavia. That's your position, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were not re-subordinated to the Army of Yugoslavia. "Re-subordination" means that they become part of its composition, that they receive tasks from them, and that they are controlled within that context, and then they are -- they are duty-bound to send reports as the others are supposed to give them orders.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's Note: Could all microphones please be switched off except for the speaker's microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Stamp, I have -- General, I shall feel very grateful if you remove one of my confusions. I quite understand that every army has it reserve force. These are people who are ex-army officials who retire and then they remain on the role to meet any emergency or meet any wartime situation. I've also learned from your discourse that there were also MUP reservists available. And all this assortment of people, reservists from both these forces, constituted the non-armed and non-Siptar population. Obviously army should be having some rules about its ex-servicemen, who remain indeed reservist position, and there should be some rule about it. And it's my understanding - I'm no expert - that obviously they will be channeling everything through the army, which is VJ in this case, and the MUP would be doing likewise, and the police, in that case. Now, if all these people were reservists, then they are drawn from these two, you see, reserves and then they are getting together. Now, keeping this background, if we read Article 63, then this talks of guards, spectrals, units of civil defence. Don't you think that the use of the reservist is something distinct from the use which is mentioned here in 63? And the reservists shall be governed by the rules and regulations of their alma mater; that's either the VJ or the MUP? I thought I should have this clarified, because you said that reservists were not such people who were just raw hands drawn from the -- from the public just at random and given arms. They were reservists. So as an expert, I think if you kindly can remove this confusion, I shall feel very grateful. Thanks a lot.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Obviously I didn't explain this right. I had hoped that I did succeed, but it seems that I didn't. The army as a system, the police as a system, the civil defence as a system. So these are subsystems of one system of defence that is called that. So the army has part of its personnel that does its military service; that is to say, conscripts doing their military service. Then there are professional officers and NCOs and civilians working in the army, and most of the units are manned from the reserve but with the exact names and surnames involved in the wartime units. Once mobilisation is declared, then they come to the mobilisation sites and then they are deployed in their respective units. Before that, they were trained in these units. They know that these are their wartime units. During 1998, as for part of the reserve force of the military, they were issued with weapons without mobilisation in order to prevent conflicts or to deal with the conflicts that had already cropped up and that were underway, as a matter of fact. The same was done by the police. The police activated their reserve forces when they deemed that necessary. The civil defence -- as for the civil defence, as for their leaders who are professionals or who are permanently employed, they're all civilians. It is only when a war occurs or if there is some kind of an emergency, then civil defence units are mobilised. So they are the only ones, the ones from the civil defence, that are civilians in the classical sense of the word. They respond to the call-up of their chain of command. So those are these three separate chains. In addition to what I've said just now, we also have the category of arming the population that does not belong to any one of these categories. We've been saying all along that there is this category as well. That category can appear only in terms of these obligations that we've been discussing; that is to say, only at a locality where they will do something that the control system of the Ministry of Defence asks them to do, but once they receive weapons they become part of the Ministry of Defence. Have I succeeded now?, in terms of improving everyone's understanding of this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: And all this then becomes a pool, you mean? Not that they work in a distinct and separate way. They become a pool, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That group has its own leader, gets its own leader. They do not become part of civil defence and civil protection units that are envisaged by establishment. A separate group is formed that has its own leader. It can be a person, an officer with a rank or without a rank but somebody who leads them. And the commander of the military unit mentioned in Article 63 carrying out activities there can appear and ask that commander, "What is it that you are doing?" Exercise some kind of control. Give some kind of advice. If necessary, make some suggestions, and so on. This is the essence of what I've been trying to explain here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sir, you said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just two -- two matters you might clarify at this stage. The -- this may be a -- an interpretation question again, but you say the groups that -- that arise spontaneously, a separate group is formed that has its own leader. It can be a person, an officer with a rank or without a rank, but somebody who leads them. How is that leader either identified or chosen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps this would be best understood if we could obtain the document, if we could see it on our screens. The document concerned is I think from June 1998, the order of Petar Ilic, the chief of the defence administration of Pristina on arming the non-Siptar population. Perhaps it would be best if we could see that, and then I could explain it on that example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the details of that, Mr. Radinovic, and it would be surprising if you as an -- if you as an expert couldn't explain the answer to what I think is a fairly simple question: How is the leader of such a group that decides action is necessary, how is he either chosen or identified?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's either someone who had already been there that is appointed. It is usually people who are quite old, over the age of 65. And one knows exactly who is who. And in that order, the chief of the administration gave instructions that every group be appointed a leader, to appoint a leader who is going to lead that group. One knows -- these are locals who know one another. You know who en enjoys what kind of -- what kind of a reputation, who served in the military or police before, who was in that line of work. People know each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And my other question is slightly detached from the line that we've been following but may be relevant to it. We've had evidence, as you know, about the movement of senior army officers out of executive positions in the army into the Ministry of Defence for various reasons. Is it possible that the line of command of the civil protection or civil defence might be headed up by a person who was a VJ officer assigned to the Ministry of Defence for a special task?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, quite certainly an officer who -- well, you know, he still -- he's still an army officer, but he is just serving in the Ministry of Defence in a position that, according to establishment, required a military officer. For example, the civil defence assistant was an officer, a general. The heads of regional organs were also officers, and they were authorised to command and control and they were trained for that, which is not to say that civilians can't be involved in this either, but they have to go through certain preparations and certain training.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your evidence about three separate lines of command or chains of command is quite clear, but one of these chains of -- or two of them effectively could be said to have connections with the Ministry of Defence, and there would appear to be the potential for overlap in -- in headquarters. Can you tell us who in 1998 and 1999 was in charge of civil protection and civil defence in the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before he was appointed of the security administration of the General Staff, this post was held by General Geza Farkas, as far as I know. He was assistant federal minister for the so-called civilian sector. The sector for civil defence. That's what it was called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: To return to the order referring to the non-Siptar population. I had suggested to you that there was no need to make specific orders in -- to civilians, to send a specific order to the civilians engaged in paragraph 5 -- or section 5 of this order. That would be done by the battalion commander on the ground. And you are saying that specific orders that have to be sent to the units and therefore paragraph 5 showed that the civilian units or the civilian population was not used. Can I ask you then: Why refer to them in paragraph 2? Why say that the assignment of the Pristina Corps is to support the MUP with reinforcements and armed non-Siptar population?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not claim that they were not used. They were used within their specific tasks, as established by the mission of the civil defence and civil protection units. What I claimed was that in Article 5 when they were not ordered what to do, they were not subordinated to the commander of the military unit. But apart from that, even when they are not subordinated to them, when they carry out tasks within their own system, the battalion commander can control them, in terms of whether they are carrying out their tasks that they were given within the mission. When they are in that zone, that is my assertion. I am not saying that they weren't doing anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And their -- their mission is to protect civilian facilities. Would you consider that, protecting civilian --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Facilities and settlements from attacks of the Siptar terrorist forces where they were encircled.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if we could look quickly, because time flows, at paragraph 76 of your report - that's page 27 - and paragraph 77. I'll just read the first sentences, two sentences of paragraph 76: "The files of the Tribunal also referred to the category of armed and non-Siptar Albanian population as an armed group. The question arises of what that is about and which category of persons was represented in this armed group and who was responsible for their arming and accordingly to whom the organisation was subordinated subordinate -- was subordinated." I'll repeat that part for emphasis: "Who was responsible for their arming and accordingly to whom that organisation was subordinated." That is how the arming of civilians of non-Siptar ethnic origin came about. And -- have you found it? Paragraph 76 is in the first section, section 1.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And paragraph 77 - I'll just read onto the record the last sentence of that - "So it is clear that these people -- these are people outside the category of conscripts and war -- with wartime assignments in some elements of the defence and security system and that they would when armed become part of the overall forces of the Federal Ministry of Defence." And I think that is your drift. It's not the VJ who is responsible for these people. It's really the Federal Ministry of Defence, where I am suggesting otherwise. I'd like us to look at P1415, bearing in mind what you have said, particularly about the arming of the -- the non-Siptar population and accordingly to whom that organisation was subordinated. If you recall, while the document is coming up - I'll just put this in context - that General Samardzic, the former commander of the 3rd Army, at the collegium minute was saying that he armed them with combat weapons, 47.000, and he armed them for a purpose, to support the VJ. General Samardzic was not speaking about civil defence and civil protection. And 1415, is it up? It's an order of the 26th of June, 1998, and it is signed by Major General Pavkovic, who was at that time General Samardzic's direct subordinate. He was then the commander of the Pristina Corps. I'd like to look at some aspects of this document. He's saying: "Pursuant to 3rd Army command, strictly confidential order of the 26th of June, 1999 [sic] and the aggravated political and security situation in Kosovo and Metohija, and in order to defend and protect citizens from the Siptar terrorist groups, I hereby order." So he refers to an order that he got from the 3rd Army from Samardzic. 1: "Organise and carry out technical preparation for distribution of weapons and ammunition to military conscripts assigned to war units of the Pristina Corps." "Distribute automatic rifle, semiautomatic rifles, light machine-guns, sniper rifles, and necessary communication equipment according to the orders of unit commanders to military conscripts, regardless of specialty." "On the basis of the list, call up small groups to arm the barracks or organise distribution of weapons in Serbian and Montenegrin villages." "Devote special attention to security measures, secrecy and camouflage discipline in carrying out this task." In 5: "Unit commanders will organise their competence training in the handling and storage and maintenance of the issued weapons." "After completing the distribution, prepare and organise inhabited places for -- for defence." If we could turn to page 2 of the English. And this is on the bottom of page 1 on the B/C/S. "Form units in each village according to military structure: In squads, platoons and companies. Appoint a commander, deputy and assistant for each unit. Organise the defence of settlements so that each settlement has sentry, patrols, ambushes, duty units, an intervention unit." And it goes on: "Place an active superior officer in charge of each settlement to directly control the preparation of units and remain there until the organisation of defence is fully completed and the unit trained." He forbids using volunteers in paragraph 8. In paragraph 10 he says: "The deadline for distribution of weapons is until 1800 hours on the 1st of July, 1999 [sic] and readiness for defence of settlements is by 1800 hours on the 3rd of July, 1998." This is dated the 26th of June, I remind you. Firstly, who commanded these village units that are armed in secrecy by the VJ? Because I suggest to you that this is what Samardzic was talking about at the collegium and this is what General Pavkovic did in accordance with General -- General Samardzic's orders. Who commanded these units?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The system of military command commanded these, because these are the reserve compositions of their units. These are not classical civilians. They are not the kind of civilians that we have been discussing. These are military conscripts with wartime assignments in the units of the Pristina Corps and the military territorial units -- or rather, the 202nd logistics base, which is a military unit. So that is not the category that we've been discussing here, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Are units based in villages?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, these are units armed by the army, its own combat units, but they were deployed in villages to protect the villages from attacks by Siptar terrorists. Siptar terrorists attacked Serbian settlements or parts of the settlements where the Serbs were in a minority.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It does not say "place the units in the villages." It says "form units in each village." These are units formed from the men of the village, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By military conscripts of combat units of the Pristina Corps. These were soldiers who were from the reserve forces of the army of the Pristina Corps that the commander, according to the approval of the army commander, mobilises and issues weapons to, and they then become part of their units. That is the establishment composition.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But you see, we have had evidence in this case - and I think in your report as well - that in mobilising for the VJ, the reserve units, A, it is not done in secrecy; and B, the VJ attempted to mobilise people from all ethnicities. Here we see a mobilisation in secrecy and a mobilisation in -- for Serbs and Montenegrin villages. This was not a typical mobilisation of VJ reservists, was it, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the conflict in Kosovo was not normal either. It's an inter-ethnic conflict, and of course it's different from a -- a classic conflict between two states. This is an internal conflict between two ethnic communities, and the army had to protect the ethnic community that was under threat and the one that was under threat was the ethnic community that was in a minority.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The minority ethnic community was protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. But you are missing the direction of my question. I'm suggesting to you that even your report - and we have had a lot of evidence of this - indicates that official mobilisation of reservists was not based on ethnicity. Here we see arming of persons in villages, training for seven days, appointing commanders of these units in the villages, done in secrecy and on the base of ethnicity. This is not typical mobilisation of the VJ reservists, is it? Simple: Is this typically the way the VJ mobilises its reserves?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not typical. It's atypical. But it's an enforced way. When the army has to replenish its ranks without declaring a state of emergency or without a public mobilisation. This is a partial mobilisation, and it's secret in order not to spread panic among the civilians and in order not to inflame the conflicts even more. That is why the commander ordered that this be done secretly, without announcing it to the public, in order not to alarm the public. Evidently this is a composition of the combat units of the Pristina Corps. This is what I am asserting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I don't want to be involved in -- in argument in all the details of what you're saying, but you seem now to be saying that this arming of men in the villages was to prevent -- was to --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not arguing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- Was not to alarm the civilian population, that is why it was done in secret. Yet in many places in your report - and we have had -- I think we have heard this before - you -- it is said that the arming of civilians in Serb villages was to give the villagers a sense of security because of the dangers of the -- the terrorists. Now you are telling us it is done in secret because you did not want to alarm the villagers?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we're talking here about two types of arming: One is issuing weapons that was quoted in this document, that is, the issuance of weapons to military conscripts who have a wartime assignment in units that issued the weapons to them. That is issuing weapons to the reservists, not to the reserve units. There are no reserve units as such. There is a part of the composition, the permanent composition, and that is replenished from the reserves, and this is what we were talking about. As to how they would be deployed, that is the prerogative of the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: General I interrupt you --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to his assessment of the security situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm sorry. I interrupted you and now, focus on my question. All I just put to you is what appears to be an inconsistency. You just said that arming VJ conscripts in secret was done not to spread alarm among the villagers. That's VJ conscripts. Whereas, you have said in your report and in the past that arming civilians in the village was done publicly in order to make them feel secure. That's all I'm putting to you. Is that not an inherent conflict?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're not talking about issuing weapons to villagers. This is military conscripts that are being issued with weapons. It's not the same thing. These are two categories of armed --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- Persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I take it your answer that to arm the conscripts, it might cause alarm. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, is it convenient to interrupt at this stage or ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. I -- I will now try to move on more quickly. I think that is appropriate, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have you any idea of --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Half hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. We need to break again, Mr. Radinovic, for about 20 minutes. Could you again leave the courtroom with the usher and we'll see you at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Just one very obvious correction to the record. On page 36, line 16 and on page 37, line 14, Mr. Stamp inadvertently referred to the dates as being 26 June 1999 and 1 July 1999. And it really is 1998. Simply for the sake of the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Mr. Stamp, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think you said the document refers to partial mobilisation of reservists, armed reservists. I would just represent to you that the document does not refer to reservists and it does not refer to mobilisation. It uses a term "military conscripts." Military conscripts, sir, are persons who have to do national service when they reach a certain age; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes and no. A military conscript is one who has already served his -- he's done his army service and is in the reservists and also someone who has yet to do his army service. The obligation starts from recruitment through military service up to serving in the reserve forces, all the way up to the age of 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If you look at paragraph 8 of this order, I'd like to point out something which I suggest would be another situation indicating that this is not referring to reservists or conscripts in the typical or regular way. It says: "I forbid formation and engagement of any volunteer units, except those comprising local village inhabitants." Volunteer units in total who were at least officially forbidden in the VJ, weren't they, at the relevant time?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Volunteers, yes, but not volunteer units. Volunteers were deployed in the various units, and then they became military conscripts, like everybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, volunteer units, which is what the section was referring to. And I think you've answered that. You -- in your report, if I may move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At paragraph 99 -- sorry, paragraph 91, where footnote 53 is... I think I -- sorry, this is, correct, paragraph 91 of the English, page 32, footnote 53. Look at the paragraph and the footnote. I think you have it before you. I won't read it, but I'll just ask you: Is my -- are you saying here that the plan Grom 98 is a basis on which the offensive in the summer and autumn of 1998 was conducted? That's anti-terrorist offensive.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a directive issued by the chief of the General Staff for the participation of the army in that anti-terrorist operation. The fight against terrorism had been ongoing before that, but this directive issued by the chief of the General Staff refers to engagement in a anti-terrorist operation. So this is the only directive we have. There had been orders in the system of command for the use of units in the fight against terrorism and to support the MUP previously, but this is the only directive covering this issue overall.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the -- the directive 4D137, is at the 28th of July, 1998. I think you have that in your report. I'd like you to look quickly at 4D101. This is an order of General Pavkovic dated 23rd of July, 1998, and it speaks of implementation of the second stage of the plan to eliminate terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija provides for the engagement of organs of the Ministry of Internal Affairs and necessary units of the PrK from the battle group in the area." So this is one of the orders in the command system for the engagement of units in the plan to combat terrorism, is it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you see it predates -- it speaks of a second stage and it predates the Grom directive. And if you look -- could look briefly at P1419. And this is an order of the 1st of August, 1998 of then-Pristina commander General Pavkovic, in which he requests approval to launch the third stage of the plan and said it was decided at a meeting of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija held on the 31st of July between 1830 and 2000 hours in the district in Pristina to launch the third stage of the plan on the 2nd of August, 1999 [sic]. And we have another document I'd like to show you. It may be not necessary. This is P2166. And I -- I believe you indicate that you had seen the document before. It's -- it's the minutes of what is called the operations interdepartmental staff for the suppression of terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija, dated 2nd of December, 1999. Have you seen this document before? I believe you indicated that you have. You haven't?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It's a rather long document, and I don't think we have time to go through all of it. If you see on the front page, these are the minutes of a meeting chaired by President Milosevic attended by President Milutinovic, Deputy Federal Prime Minister Sainovic, General Perisic, General Dimitrijevic, General Samardzic, General Pavkovic, General Djordjevic of the MUP, and Major General Lukic of the MUP, among others. And at that meeting, Pavkovic, if you look at the bottom of page 1 of the B/C/S, which is the top of page 2 of 2 English, General Pavkovic speaks -- and I quote now - "Speaking on behalf of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija, General Pavkovic reminded the members of the operation staff that the plan for suppressing terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija have been carried out in five stages with an overall duration of 45 to 55 days. Implementation of the plan commenced on the 25th of July and the activities were completed by the 29th of October." So here we have -- if and if you go on to other part I refer to is page 7 of the English, which is also page 7 in the B/C/S version, in which Major General Lukic submitted a report on the work of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija devoting special attention to the highly professional successful cooperation between the army and the police commands and units in performing the following tasks, and he refers to the tasks. And he also at page 8 of the B/C/S but the same page in the English, he -- at the end of his report, General Lukic agreed with the assessments and positions set out by the command of the VJ of the Pristina Corps, General Pavkovic. At paragraph 161, I think it is, of -- of the report. May I just check this. No, it's -- it is not paragraph 161. Yes, it is paragraph 161, but I think it is in part -- part 2. Paragraph 161, page 120 of the English, you speak about probably -- you say "probably" -- it indicates apparently that you are speculating here -- "the relations between the MUP and the VJ was for the most part based on the principle of cooperation and coordination and that there might have been some ad hoc set-up coordinating body," and I think earlier in answer to questions from Judge -- Judges Chowhan and Bonomy about what happened on the ground, how could things coordinate on the ground, you said you did analyse that in your report, what we see here that you speculate -- or you say probably this was the situation. The question is this: When you have persons of the level of General Pavkovic and General Lukic making reports about joint operations on the ground in Kosovo to the command of the VJ -- well, firstly, to President Milosevic, President Milutinovic, Deputy President Sainovic, and the commanders of the VJ, wouldn't you agree with me that that coordinating body would have had effectively on the ground binding authority over the units involved on the ground even if there was no formal subordination of the units? I shouldn't say "binding authority." I should say "effective control." I think that's a bit -- sir, let me rephrase that. Where the chief command of the police in Kosovo, General Lukic; commander of the army in Kosovo, General Pavkovic, reports to people of that rank in the country about the coordination on the ground in Kosovo, wouldn't the body that commanded them and that coordinated their activities have effective control over these units on the ground even if there was no formal subordination of these units to that body?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask for Mr. Stamp to identify where he is getting the phrase "chief command of the police in Kosovo" for Mr. Lukic. Time and again we've had to address this issue because of the issues of translation and the misuse of words. The title for Mr. Lukic was "Rukovodilac Staba MUP-a," which has a certain meaning, and that meaning is not as a chief, which would be a "nacelnik," or as a commander, which would be a "komandant" or "komandir." So I would object to this question on the grounds that it's misrepresenting facts asking and, therefore, asking the witness to speculate on matters that are not in evidence in the manner that Mr. Stamp is presenting them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, give me the English for the first of these expressions that he used.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: "Rukovodilac," if you might recall from our 98 bis submissions, I presented the dictionary definition, of this which was director or organiser or head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I imagine "head" will do for Mr. Stamp's purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct. And as a -- as a further correction, he indicate who is was present. I believe this document indicates that the Minister of the Interior, Stojilkovic, was present; the assistant minister, Obrad Stevanovic; and the deputy minister and head of the RJB, Mr. -- General Djordjevic were also present, at least on the RJB side. I don't recall if any RDB personnel were also listed as being present. But I think we have to -- if we're going to ask for speculation, we have to least try and minimise the speculation by specifying exactly the parameters upon which the speculation is based. And if this document is the bases for the speculation being sought by Mr. Stamp, I think he need to accurately reflect what's in here instead of twisting it, as I submit the Prosecution has also done in the past, take things out of context and twisting them to get a further twisted speculation that does not help anyone in this case get any closer to the truth-seeking that ought to be prevailing in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic there, are two separate issues here. There's the exact role played by Mr. Lukic and there is the question whether this meeting -- or the -- the -- the reporting was coming from the top brass of the police and the top brass of the army. Now, if we take that general global description of the personnel as the most senior officials for the army and the police, do you accept that approach?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If Mr. Stamp accurately reflects within his documents. So far he has not mention the leadership of the police except for mentioning Mr. Lukic and implying that Mr. Lukic is the leadership of the police. That's the crux of my objection, that he's misrepresenting both the evidence that is through this exhibit and the evidence that's been presented and led in this case through other exhibits and other witnesses. So I -- I think that if -- if he's going to ask such a convoluted and compound question, I think he needs to break it down and stick to what is actually presented here to -- to have this -- this exercise have any meaning that could lead us to have any kind of result that would be of benefit to the Trial Chamber in reaching its ultimate determinations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, when I referred to -- to the names of the person who attended, I said inter alia to encompass all of the other persons present. At that time, the document was in front of the witness with the names of all the person who is attended, so he could see it. As far as he said about twisting the Prosecution, the Prosecution twisted, et cetera, I'm not going to be engaged in that sort of exchange. I wouldn't indicate it that way. I will just say this: The -- no, I -- I don't think I'll get into that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
