utterances.text: Well, you can take it and Mr. Ivetic can take it as well that we do not consider that the formulation of questions by you in the context of this cross-examination has at any stage amounted to deliberate twisting or misleading of the -- twisting of the evidence or misleading of the witness about the evidence. The question of just how accurate the formulation of the question is is -- is quite another matter. But the way we see this question at the moment is that it relates to the general situation of the senior officials in army and police reporting to others. Now, it might be best, in view of what's happened, that -- for you to rephrase the question in as concise a form as you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: General, I think you probably understand the question, but I will -- see, where you have a situation where the leaders of the army and the police are reporting to the -- to the top echelons of the state about the coordinated -- coordinated engagement of the police and the army in Kosovo, then as an expert wouldn't it be that this coordinating body would have had effective control of those units in Kosovo even if there was not an official document re-subordinating these units to the coordinated body?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, I think one point should be clarified. Paragraph 161 of the witness's report presents two alternatives. The expert provides two options.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's -- that's not a matter for you to intervene on at this stage. If in some way your client is prejudiced by the way this is approached, you will be given an opportunity of further cross-examination. Is the question clear in your mind, Mr. Radinovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you then answer it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I have not seen this document before, so I cannot base my answer on the document, but in answer to the question as to whether "coordination" implies a conclusion on effective control, my opinion is no, it doesn't. "Coordination" means exactly what it says. There is a body coordinating the activities of two subsystems working on the same task. When the tasks of each side are coordinated and it's established who should be doing what and what they should be doing separately and what they should be doing together, then each system controls its own part. There can be no effective control by someone over forces that are not under his command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. I agree that there can be no effective control if they are not to some degree under your control. However - and I ask you this for your opinion as an expert - if the people in charge of these two units, two different chains of command, are reporting on the success of the units to the top echelons of the state and the army and the police, isn't it reasonable to conclude, sir, as an expert that the ad hoc coordinating body that you say probably existed, in paragraph 161 of your report, had effective command-and-control competencies on the ground?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. No, it could not have effective command-and-control competencies by any means, because that would imply a well-developed system of command and control. It would mean that there was a system of reporting in existence. Because how could they exercise control unless they received daily reports and issued daily orders. And evidently --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Without --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or rather, in this material, I do not have grounds to conclude anything else except for what I've said. Of course, I am basing my conclusion not only on what you asked me just now but on everything that I studied for my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. But in the circumstances -- circumstance that I have described, even without formal re-subordination and a -- and formal reporting up and formal reporting down, wouldn't this coordinating body have de facto control if that coordinating body or the leaders of that coordinating body were reporting to the leaders of the police, the army, and the state? Wouldn't it have de facto effective control on the ground? In your opinion.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each military commander individually has the control of -- of his system and his unit, and the police official has the control of his, but the coordination body does not imply that complete control is established, because this is simply not possible. Coordination is the lowest level, the lowest level of establishing any types of relationships between the different systems. I understand that here we're talking about two separate systems, and since they are in the same area, they find themselves in the same area and often are performing the same tasks, then coordination was quite a natural procedure. "Coordination," this means that -- and "coordination" means that the military commander and the police officer would find themselves in that coordinating body and that they would mutually inform each other about what was being done, and they would review what would need to be done in the future and then everyone would need to do their part of the job, without effective control that you are talking about. That simply is not possible like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I am not sure if you focused on what I asked, but I have to move on for time. You said, in respect to the reporting chain, that General Ojdanic was diligent in ensuring that there was timely and accurate reporting, that he devoted exceptional attention to that. Did you see in various collegium minutes in 1999, General, at those meetings, telling General Ojdanic that a lot of the reporting that he was getting, primarily from the 3rd Army, was inaccurate or alleged to be inaccurate? Did you see reports of that nature?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said "General Ojdanic," and you're talking about inaccurate reports. I assume we are actually talking about General Dimitrijevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. I'm saying General Dimitrijevic --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Andjelkovic raised it at one time in a different collegium meeting that there might be misleading reports coming from the 3rd Army, and this was before the 24th of March, 1999. So you saw that. Do you know of any steps General Ojdanic took to correct the situation in respect to reporting from the 3rd Army prior to the 24th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there was an inspection carried out in early May 1999 that was personally handled by General Ojdanic, march. And he personally wanted to see what the situation was in the field. And then there were plenty of orders that required specific reporting of data that had been checked, of accurate data. The general was quite generous in his demands.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know if any disciplinary steps were taken in respect to the commander of the 3rd Army or any investigations were conducted in respect of the 3rd Army in respect to these allegations?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the material that was available to me, I did not conclude that there was a sufficient reason to initiate anything in the sense that you are going. There was no grounds for the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command to undertake any disciplinary measures in relation to the command of the -- of the commander of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, I think I can assume from that answer that you are saying that notwithstanding these reports from his colleagues at the collegium, General Ojdanic did not take any steps to indicate -- to investigate the 3rd Army command and the reporting from the 3rd Army. Your answer is "no"?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, his answer is not "no." He answered it and told him exactly what steps he took. He sent an inspection team down there and issued certain orders. So Mr. Stamp can't go back and say "your answer to my question is no." It was not "no." It was yes. He did take specific steps and found there was nothing to discipline about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is not even appropriate. But I am speaking about investigation. I just asked the witness about investigations and the answer he gives appears to be reasons why there are no investigations. And I just want to confirm on the record whether or not his answer means no, there were no observations. What concerns is to -- to is put a comment which was not necessary even in making the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think the problem is caused by the earlier answer at line 7 of page 54, where there is reference to an inspection carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, there is reference to an inspection. I'm asking about investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I take it from your last answer, Witness, when you said that there were, in your view, no grounds for an investigation, you are saying that there were no investigations, as far as you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let the witness answer, Mr. Ackerman. You can clarify the position if there's something inappropriate emerges. Please answer that question, Mr. Radinovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From what I know, there were no investigations in the classic sense. There were no investigations in the sense of what I would understand to be an investigation. But there were controls, inspections, tours, reports. Quite enough relevant sources about -- in order to be able to assess what was being done there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours, for your kindness in indulging me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There is one answer that you could perhaps clarify for us. You -- when you were saying that you knew there was an inspection carried out in early 1999 and you went on to say there were plenty of orders that required specific reporting that had to be checked of accurate data, the -- you then said: "The general was quite generous in his demands." At least, that's the English translation. Is that what you actually said?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was generating a lot of requests that called for accurate, correct, and precise reporting in. In Serbian, you would use the term "exacting" perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, from what I recall - and the witness said in paragraph 56, line 22, he said "no," and then he explained what he meant. So his answer did not begin with a "yes" but with a "no," and then he went on to explain. But I think that this was understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, I -- I think we've got the picture. Thank you, Mr. Visnjic. There are a number of areas in which you may be able to help us, Mr. Radinovic. We have heard a great deal about a body called the collegium. Can you tell us, please, what the -- or who the collegium comprised. Who were its members?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The collegium comprised first the subordinated assistants or heads of the sections or independent administrations. In order to avoid confusion, what are independent administrations? These would be the administrations that were not in sectors but were directly connected to the Chief of the General Staff or the chief of the staff of the General Command; that was the security administration, for example, the intelligence administration. These were the -- the independent administrations that had direct connections to the chief of the staff. So this would be the innermost leadership part. So the collegium was a body, but it can also imply a method of work; meaning that when this body made of the innermost assistants is -- discuss the most essential and crucial questions that have to do with the working of the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've also heard evidence that the individual members would arrange for a deputy to attend on their behalf if -- if they were unable to attend. Is that your understanding?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether collegium meetings would normally always involve everyone falling into the category you've mentioned or whether, depending on the agenda, it would be a more restricted group which would meet.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the factual state of affairs in order to be able to give you a direct answer, but what I think is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. I -- I think it's better if you -- if you don't tell us just what you think or speculate about, because I think from memory, your own direct experience of the General Staff is limited to the mid-1980s.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1984. Yes, the 1980s, the direct experience. But I was a member of the collegium of the Federal Ministry of Defence, so perhaps that experience is not to be discarded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Not to be discarded, but we've heard from so many people who were directly involved in these meetings, that I think it would be unwise to press you further on the factual position. During the -- the collegium met on a regular basis during peacetime. From your researches, can you tell us how frequent these meetings were? And that's prior to the 24th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once a week most frequently. Sometimes even more. As needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: During the conflict, there were apparently daily meetings. They've generally speaking, been referred to here in evidence as "briefings." How do these compare with meetings of the collegium?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are two methods of work. Most often what would happen was that both the collegium and the briefings would be attended by the same people, but the collegium was a method of work that was occasional, once a week or more frequently, as needed; while the briefings were a method of work that occurred on a daily basis. There would be a briefing on the situation every day, on the situation in the army units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: As far as you can tell from your research, did the same personnel attend each briefing?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, yes. I'm not sure that it would always be the same people, but generally, yes, it would be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And can you tell us if definitely there were collegium meetings during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Bearing in mind that there were daily briefings during the conflict, what was it that was discussed at collegium meetings during that period?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the collegium meetings -- the collegium meetings usually reviewed general questions that were of importance not only for that day or the specific situation in the military but also that had some lasting significance and were of a general nature. For example, personnel matters, appointments, the problem of material financial provisions. Let's say when there were reviews, the collegium which preceded the directive of the 9th of April regarding the engagement of the army. So whenever there was a need to review an important question of lasting significance was something that was done at the collegium. The briefings usually would deal with the situation on the front.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wonder if we could have on the screen 3D728 and page 3 in the English, where it sets out those present at the meeting. Now, we need to go to the bottom of the page and find the equivalent in the B/C/S. You may have to see more of this document. Are you familiar with it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was one of the briefings, judging by the type of document, I think it was a briefing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, the part that's on the screen indicates the presence of President Milosevic and President Milutinovic, and he probably hates it every time he sees this, but Second Lieutenant Sainovic. Now, how -- how often -- that indicates obviously a civilian political presence at this meeting. How often was there such --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, can you clarify for me where it is and when it is that Milosevic, Milutinovic, and Sainovic were present.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look just below where it says "Colonel General Ojdanic," it says -- there are two dashes, one of them says "in the course of the evening, corrections of directives compared to ours," meaning the version that they already have. The second dash: "Submit the draft plan for study. The briefing willing be at 0900 hours with the Supreme Command present." And then the "present" paragraph refers only to those who were present at the briefing; meaning that the briefing regarding the plan would be attended by the deputy of the operations and staff affairs, chief of the operations administration, chief of the Supreme Command Staff, Air Force General Smiljanic, so those who would be able to provide additional explanation to the Supreme Commander and the Supreme Command, if needed, would be present. So what was being reviewed here was the plan of -- for the engagement of forces. So these people were not present at the briefing, but the civilians were supposed to be briefed on the topic that was discussed at the briefing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that was to take place at 9.00 the following day.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just one intervention in the transcript the witness said 61, 6: "Submit the brief will be at 900 hours at the Supreme Commander." That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. However, what we have here is a meeting at which a number of the senior military personnel would meet together with senior political figures. Now, you -- you told us yesterday that there were daily briefings of the Supreme Commander by the chief of the General Staff or the -- the Supreme Command Staff. And this -- this looks like one of these meetings. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is more than that. This is more than the daily meeting where the Chief of the General Staff would brief on the military -- on the combat report of the army. What this was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That helps me to formulate the question, which is: How often, as far as your researches discovered, did meetings of the nature of this intended meeting at 9.00 take place? In other words, meetings of similar groupings of military -- senior military and senior political figures.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rarely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, can you be more precise than that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the only one that I identified. I didn't see any others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were you invited when you were preparing your report to consider at all a term which has cropped up often in this case, "the Joint Command"?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Explicitly, no. I received a general -- I will answer, if you permit me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Well, I -- I really want to be cautious about what I ask you about this. I -- I want your comment on one particular issue. It's obvious from what you've already said that you've heard of the expression "the Joint Command." I'm correct in that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Right. Now --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You concluded correctly, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is very much a question for your expertise and experience as a senior military officer. If you received a document which contains suggestions from a more senior officer, would that be a -- a format of document you would understand, expect to receive?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you have in your career received such documents, have you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The witness who spoke most recently about this, General Curcin, said he had only ever seen one, the particular one which was presented in the case, but they are a regular feature of military life, are they?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was not something that was a regular feature. In the army, the most frequent form of communication are orders, reports, information, commands. Suggestions are not something that occur very frequently. It's -- it's something that is done infrequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you were to receive such a document, or indeed any other more formal document of the type you've just described, and that document made it clear that it was linked in some way to something called "the Kosovo and Metohija Joint Command order, strictly confidential, number 455-148 of 15 April 1999," would that cause you to ask questions about that source document or linked document?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you expect any senior military officer faced with a document saying that to -- to ask himself what exactly that was?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because in that document what appears is -- well, in that document, what is invoked is some order that he did not issue. And it's addressed to his subordinate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, could we then have on the screen, please, P1487. Could you assist us by -- by giving your opinion on -- on how you see that -- these two documents fitting into the command structures that you've been describing to us? And by "the two documents," I mean the suggestions document, which is P1487, and the link, the joint command order.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, believe me, it would be hard for me to establish a link here. I have seen this document. I did see this document. The document that this suggestion refers to is one with a number that, as far as I know, from the abundance of documents that I've looked at and analysed, are derived from the staff of the Pristina Corps. 455 is the number that comes from that corps. So my conclusion is that this is a document and this is a reference to a document that was technically, at least, created and registered in the logbook or the operations logbook of the command of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what I infer or conclude on the basis of what is written here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that immediately raises the question: In the Pristina Corps, what was the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Joint Command? Well, actually, irrespective of that, how we answer the question, whether it existed or whether it did not exist - I don't think it existed, but I have arguments to support that - but anyway, no matter what kind of an answer that give to that question, the document was created in the Pristina Corps why they called it "the Joint Command" I really don't understand. I cannot answer that question. Why a name was given to something that it cannot bear, not according to any rule of military doctrine. That, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: My particular concern about this is -- is the matter I raised at the outset with you. I appreciate the limitations on your ability to deal with this organisation, whatever it was, and my concern is this: That we have heard evidence from a very large number of generals in the Yugoslav Army who have been asked about the expression "Joint Command" and they've given us the impression that it was neither here nor there what this body was. The -- they -- they weren't alerted in any particular way by this use of the expression "Joint Command" to think, What on earth is this? Has somebody made a mistake? Should we inquire about it? Does this make sense to you that all these officers should just dismiss this as of no significance?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That there was coordination is something that we've been convinced of in many cases. It really was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm not sure that you're answering my question. I -- I want to focus on this question: What would you expect the reaction of a senior army officer to be to seeing this expression? Because of the word "command" in particular but also because it's said to be a "Joint Command," which is something you've dismissed, you yourself have also dismissed as just not existing within the system.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand this to mean that a suggestion is made to this body that coordinates the activities of the MUP and the army in order to have this coordinated activity organised in the best possible way. That is how I understand this. The Chief of the Supreme Command Staff knows that there is a coordinating body that coordinates the work of the MUP and the army. And, since in this document that he had seen, he found some things that he thought were not right, he is making a suggestion in terms of what should be done in order to have this activity carried through properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you haven't answered my question. And I -- I will come back it to, but what is it, then, that was the coordinating body?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these are people who were there on the spot, who were discussing matters coordinating the work of the MUP and the army. In the field and on the ground, where there was coordinated activity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you're not telling us that there is a -- a body that is actually coordinating activity in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this coordination between the MUP and the army. The MUP and the army. These are officers of the MUP, officers of the army. It is probably some of the politicians on the ground. So it's that coordination that is established on the ground. This type of coordination existed at all levels, even down at brigade level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who are the politicians on the ground who are involved in this?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably the people who were down there on the ground: The president of the executive council, then this -- well, in this other document before I saw Minic, the president of that -- that council of citizens. So it is officers of the MUP, officers of the army, and at a joint meeting they familiarise each other with each other's activities and they reach agreement on what the most efficient way to proceed would be in the following period, and then everybody does his own work. Those who made -- or rather, the person who made the suggestions sees that something went wrong in the activity that was conceived and he's trying to do something about it. That is how I understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you're -- you're referring back now to the document Mr. Stamp showed you towards the end, which was the interdepartmental staff minutes. Is that what -- is that what you're talking about now?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am mentioning this document that he showed me by way of an illustration. It can look like coordination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But -- but what's clear is it doesn't have in it the words "Joint Command." Now, I'll go back to the question I was asking you, which is whether you would expect senior officers in the Yugoslav Army who saw the word "Joint Command" or the -- the expression "Joint Command" to dismiss it as an expression of no significance, that they didn't need to make any inquiry about the nature of. Does that -- does that make sense to you in a -- in a --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't make any sense. I assume that they knew exactly what this was all about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just -- just to be clear, although I think you may have answered this already: This document that's still on the screen involves suggestions down the chain of command, rather than up the way. That -- that is also normal, is it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not a frequent occurrence, but yes, it is done, especially if two systems appear in the same, well, activity. The Chief of the Supreme Command Staff makes a suggestion here but only to the commander of the 3rd Army, although he invokes this document of the so-called Joint Command, he gives suggestions to his subordinate. And he sends suggestions to the command of the 3rd Army, not to a Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Turning to something else now. The reporting system to the General Staff during the conflict involved daily reporting. Was the system prior to the conflict similar or was reporting then on a less-regular basis?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In peacetime and in wartime, reporting takes place on a daily basis. In peacetime, operations reports were sent; and in wartime, combat reports were sent, daily reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think in -- in fairness to you, to ensure that -- and indeed to the other witnesses in the case, and to ensure that you have the whole picture, you should see P1878. This is the linked order that was numbered 455-148. Can you just glance quickly at each of the pages. There are about five pages. It's difficult to read. Yes, it's small.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could it please be zoomed in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll quickly print a hard copy for you so you can read it quickly. I don't want you to read all the detail. Just to get the -- the format in your mind. And a hard copy will be given to you for that purpose. Now that you have that, we could put back on the screen P1439. I'm sorry? Oh, sorry. Sorry. I've given you the wrong number there. Sorry, 1487. It's just in case you want to make any other comment about how these two fit together within the appropriate military structures that you've been describing.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from the letterhead, the name "Joint Command," all the rest that is written in the document was done precisely in accordance with how combat documents are created and all the wording is very correct in keeping with military terminology and military doctrine. As for the structure and the formulations, I would have no objections. I just have this dilemma, why it's called "Joint Command" and why in the signature it says "Joint Command" when it all pertains to the Pristina Corps. Quite simply that, is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you read paragraph number 13, the second sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's Note: We do not have the text in front of us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, that's -- it seems to the layman, which in these matters we are, to be a straightforward statement that some organisation called the Joint Command is in charge of all the forces involved in this operation. Why should we not read it that way?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because in order for something to be a command, it has to correspond to that name. It has to have -- it has to receive reports from someone. It has to be seen that this someone is subordinated to them. Also, they have to have their logbook, because these documents are kept according to a special procedure in operations logbooks, not like just any element of official correspondence. These are documents that are kept permanently. There should be a signature. There should be a stamp. This cannot be the stamp of a Joint Command, and not the number either. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What about -- what about the possibility that the command structure just wasn't working; it was being bypassed?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. We have hundreds of documents that show that the commander of the Pristina Corps and the 3rd Army were functioning precisely as prescribed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Supreme Command is receiving reports from the army. There are no reports from a Joint Command. There is not a single order addressed to the Joint Command. Quite simply, quite simply that is something that to the best of my knowledge did not exist as a command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now could you look, please, at P1439. Now, you'll see that the paragraph numbered 1 starts with the words "contrary to your orders." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And if you could then go down to the second paragraph under number 2, that starts with "on my return." Could you read that just slowly to me, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Upon my return from the briefing to the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija on the 19th and 20th of September, 1998, with a decision on the establishment of the rapid deployment forces, I acquainted you with that personally over the telephone."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, how -- how do you read this situation?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for what is called "Joint Command" here, well, as it is being called, I said why I think that this does not exist as a Joint Command. The corps commander is addressing the army commander and informing him that at this meeting of this body a decision was made to create a rapid deployment force and he is asking for support there too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But he's -- he seems to be acting contrary to the orders he has had from his own superior, which is the way you've told us the system must always work; you must always get your orders from the man who's in your chain of command.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the basis of this, one can conclude that the commander of the army did not allow the establishment of the rapid deployment force although it was decided at the coordination meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But does it not look as though General Pavkovic just went ahead and did it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he probably proposed that because the combat groups that had been established earlier were engaged in other tasks and there would be a need to intervene and there aren't any appropriate forces for that; hence, his request to have that kind of force created.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, what is then your understanding of the expression "the reporting session of the Joint Command," bearing in mind you've told us there's no evidence of any reporting system?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I quite simply understand this to mean that they met at a meeting - that is to say, officers of the army and the police - and this number of politicians who were there then, and that they were talking about who was doing what and what should be done, and that it was agreed there that a rapid-deployment force would be established. Obviously the commander of the 3rd Army did not accept that, as one can see from this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we also see from this document that he was overruled?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you cannot see that this was annulled, but since he raises the question again, certainly the army commander did not accept this. Or rather, I assume that he did not accept this, but I'm not sure. It cannot be stated with certainty on the basis of this document. But since he is asking for this, the assumption is that it was not accepted. Had this been a Joint Command, then the army commander would not have refused that. He'd have to carry it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's time for a break, I think. Mr. Visnjic, are you likely to have extensive re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I still have a number of questions, though, and will occupy a significant part of the remaining time. Mr. Stamp, for you does anything arise out of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Not for the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And Mr. Petrovic, anything arise for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe the answer is yes, there will be questions from our side, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think so. One of us will have...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have to have a break for half an hour and we'll resume at 1.00. Could you meanwhile leave the courtroom again with the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Radinovic, in paragraph 65 of your report -- now, it's paragraph 65 of the -- certainly the English section is page 90, where you're dealing with the question of the Supreme Command Staff's position in the chain of command. Do you have paragraph 65?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You refer there to -- you refer to command responsibility and control responsibility. What's the difference between these?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Control" is a broader term than "command." "Control" implies the process, functions of planning, organising.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And in the broader sense, command is part of control, but "command" is a narrower term and it implies the right to issue orders and implies the strict duty of subordinates to execute those commands. So that is "command." "Control" is a broader term, and it does not have such a strict command function in the same way that "command" has. Although, they are often used as synonyms, but they are not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise for interrupting you, but I would just like to draw attention to a problem that may appear later when we analyse. The witness uses the term here "rukovodjenje," which is translated into English as "control." In Serbian there is another term, "kontrola," which is narrower than the term command "komandovanje," command. So I don't want later while analysing the transcript to have any inconsistencies. So we have the situation here that two terms in Serbian - one is "rukovodjenje," the other term is "kontrola" - are interpreted or translated into English as the same word. This happened yesterday also in the transcript, and today I would like possibly to have a certain revision of the transcript so that in a way we can differentiate that in the event that we cannot find an adequate term in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that will be considered. The Chamber can reflect on that after today by looking at that part of the evidence and Mr. Haider will remind us about that at the beginning of the week. Can I turn now to a concept you referred to as "the operations centre," and you talk also of "the operations duty team." Is the operations centre a place or a body of people?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a place and a group of people that works at that place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what is the difference between the personnel of the operations centre and the operations duty team, or are they the same?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are not the same thing. Operations centre, in the organisational and personnel terms, is part of the operations administration of the General Staff or the first administration of the General Staff; and that is a body or a point, location, that functions continuously, and it serves for the operational connections of the system of command from top to bottom. So from the brigade to the General Staff, operations centres are established and the General Staff have -- has its own operational centre, which is part of the operations administration. Now, operations duty. Operations duty is organised at all these levels that I mentioned, from the brigade up to the General Staff, whereby the -- we have operations duty officers in brigades and at higher levels we have operations duty teams. In the General Staff, the operations duty team is led by the officer the rank of a general, so that in the professional sense he could cover what is important for the military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And -- excuse me. The operations duty team is not part of the operations centre. It's -- it uses the resources of the operations centre, but in personnel terms it's not part of it. It changes. Most frequently the leader of the operations duty team is one of the assistants of the Chief of the General Staff or of the section or department within the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think it follows from what you have said that the operations centre of the General Staff simply became the operations centre of the Supreme Command Staff when war broke out.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does it also follow from what you've said that there's an operations duty team at each of the command posts throughout the command structure? Or in fact, it doesn't. Sorry, you did make it clear. There's an operations duty team in the command post of only the -- the higher levels; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. And --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But at all levels of the army, from the brigade, then -- that's where they all have the operations duty officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, I'm -- I've caused this confusion myself. From brigade level downwards - is that what you're saying? - it's only a -- a duty officer and a team is above that level? No. Could you explain again, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Beginning from the brigade upwards, you have the operations duties. In the brigade, you have the operations duty officer and then upwards, corps army General Staff, you would have the operations duty team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you've been asked a number of questions about the personnel who form the fighting force. Excuse me. And we find an element of confusion in some of the expressions used. And -- and one today that you use but give a very wide definition to was conscript. Now, tell me again what a conscript was in the Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A military conscript is a person subject to military duty. And now I have to explain what military duty is. The military duty encompasses recruiting of young men who are from 17 years old. These men are entered into the military records as recruits. Recruiting, as part of the military duty, implies the selection and classification, medical checks, assessment of physical abilities, psychophysical tests, so getting a -- a psychological and physical profile of a young recruit. And this is also something that includes education, affinities, qualities, and that's how young men are recruited for specific services and arms of duty. When they become 19 or when we have young men who are studying, then when they reach 27 years of age, they are summoned to serve their military term of duty. That is the next segment of military duty, to serve their term of office. When they serve they -- their term, the soldier is entered into the records of the reserve forces, and he's assigned, according to his military specialty that he has been trained for, he's entered into the records of the appropriate military units according to their specialty. And occasionally they're invited for professional training of the reserve forces. That is also part of the military duty and, of course, that also implies the duty to respond to the mobilisation call, as needed. So that would be the whole of the military duty, what that term implies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: At what age do they undergo the basic training?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 19 to 20, depending on how long the military term of duty is. Now it's six months. Before that it used to be a year. So this is done between the ages of 19 and 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've heard occasional reference to professional soldiers. Were there professional soldiers in the Yugoslav Army?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These would be professional officers, commissioned and non-commissioned officers. These would be civilians serving in the military and soldiers serving under contract, so soldiers, people whose only job that was, who have a contract and are carrying out their duties as professional soldiers. Unfortunately, that number is quite small. We are still not in the position to replenish our army with professional personnel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the latest age at which a conscript could be mobilised?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 60 is the latest age, but it depends on the type of unit. Of course, elite units would not be replenished with older people, but they would be replaced differently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was 60 the -- the rule in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've had a number of references in evidence to operations known as Grom and some numbers associated with these. And I think you have given evidence about these as well. I wonder if you could have a look, please, at P1221. This -- you haven't got it in your language yet. Yes. This document refers to something known as Operation Grom or Thunder between 29th May 1998 and 20th of June, 1998. Now, that seems to be something different from the Operation Grom which had parts 1 -- a phase 1 and phase 2 in July. Do you know anything about this particular Operation Grom?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know of Operation Grom that was mentioned in the General Staff directive of the 28th of July. I don't know about this one here that is specifically mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And there are other documents dated earlier in July, the 22nd, which make reference to the plan for combatting terrorist forces. Are you aware of those documents?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you look now, please, at P939. Now, this is a -- a minute of the collegium. And if you could go to page 35 in the English. I can't, I'm sorry, give you a B/C/S page. But in this - I can simply narrate it to you just now - in it there is reference by Colonel Vlajkovic to the disengagement of units in Operation Mac, M-a-c, followed by the word "Sword" -- sorry, I've pronounced that wrong, the Operation Mac, and then it's followed by the word "Sword," which may be a translation of Mac, so in English, Operation Sword. Does that mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was an operation that was planned at the time when eight members of the army were kidnapped when the Siptar terrorist forces carried out the kidnapping and the General Staff was planning a measure in case the negotiations failed to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... That fits in -- that fits in with other information and does clarify the position. And on the subject of names, just one other question: In a document in August 1998, which is P1423, there is reference to a unit called the Brazil Unit. Does that mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's an exotic name of some police force or special group, but no. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The -- the actual sentence in the -- it's a report -- says: "The MUP force engaged consisted of the 1st and 2nd MUP Detachments, the SAJ, and the Brazil Unit." It means --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I don't know that there were Brazil units in our police. No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where a MUP unit is re-subordinated to a VJ unit for an operation, was it the responsibility of the MUP -- the VJ commander to deal with the punishment of any member of the MUP who committed a crime in the course of the operation?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A MUP unit is subordinated to the military commander for specific combat tasks, only that part of the unit that is taking part in the combat action, and that unit is subordinated, just like any other unit would be. But if it is established that a member of the police unit carried out a criminal act, then that case would be reported and it would be resolved within the MUP control system, not the military commander's duty. It would end at that point when they reported to the MUP senior officials that this matter needed to be investigated. He's not authorised to take measures when we're talking about attached units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you're saying here an obligation, at least to draw the matter to the attention of the MUP authorities.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What about the other element of preventing a crime? If -- if the VJ commander has reason to think that a crime may be committed by one of the forces subordinated to him and one of the MUP forces, what is then his responsibility?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is the potential possibility for that kind of inappropriate behaviour, both on the part of the members of the military and the members of the police, and the commander is obliged to do everything possible to prevent something like that from happening. That means that he needs to issue orders, to supervise, to react. If he knows that something like that was done or if that is within his range, that he's able to act. And if a unit is subordinated to the military unit, everything that he is obliged to do in relation to his unit, he is obliged to do in relation to the MUP units, other than them being charged with criminal responsibility. That is not in his domain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there now anything arising that you wish to examine further on, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No. I'm having something checked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. If following any questions by Mr. Zecevic or Mr. Petrovic then you -- you wish to raise anything, then you need to draw that to my attention. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We have no questions, and neither does --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't have questions either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I could have gone another 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I just wanted to -- just for the record, Your Honour, when you were going through the questions you asked about the -- the suggestions series of documents, there's a third document in that series that I think is important to understanding that whole drama, and that's 4D420, which the witness was not asked to explain if -- I don't know whether you want to go into that or not. I don't want to, but I think the Chamber should at least be aware of the existence of that document. Just to remind you, that's a document I raised with Curcin. It's Pavkovic's response to that suggestions document from Ojdanic where he explains that it wasn't received and couldn't be implemented because it was a MUP operation, in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. No, I'm content, Mr. Ackerman, with the questions that have been raised. Thank you very much, though. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to add, Your Honours, that document is footnote 206 in the expert report of General Radinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, Mr. Radinovic, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming to give evidence and for the assistance you've given us. You're now free to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic -- Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, Mr. Visnjic has kindly assigned to me the privilege of ending General Ojdanic's case, which we now do, subject, of course, to the motions regarding the exhibits, to the Court's ruling on exhibits. There'll be two brief motions filed today, again with reference to the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, everything should be before us by the end of today. And subject to anything you've raised by then, your case will be closed. I'm curious about one matter, just in case there is any oversight here. At one stage you promised us a handwriting expert. "Promise" is setting it too high.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did, and we shall work on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And it's probably going to be a joint witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Joint with whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, probably a few Defence teams, and perhaps even the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But it -- my understanding of this is it's an issue between you and Mr. Ackerman. And if I've got that right, I assume he would not be part of the joint criminal enterprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have to ask Mr. Ackerman that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, if -- if -- the issue, as I understand it, is -- is in relation to documents that he is concerned about. And if you have a -- a joint position, you don't need a witness. The only reason you would need a witness would be if there was something you couldn't jointly declare to us as accepted by everybody in the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as I understand things, we still haven't got a joint position on this. But, of course, that is subject to further debate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you seeking therefore, Mr. Sepenuk, that the case is closed subject also to that issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And others, Your Honour. There are other joint witnesses; for example --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: -- We have an expert witness with relation to the testimony given by Patrick Ball. So obviously our case remains open subject to that testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And there are two expert witnesses that we know about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But there is a difference in a situation where we don't know about a witness, albeit he's an expert. So you're asking us to qualify the closure of your case by reference to the possibility of a witness who will speak as an expert about handwriting. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic is the handwriting expert, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Your Honour. And in that context, I just wish to remind you that we submitted a request to the government of Serbia for, I hope, this time a comprehensive written version of the reports on evening briefings. So I'm waiting for that and perhaps some more subsequent evidence, and we will address the Court in due course when we get such material. So I assume that there will be some other uncertainties in the future, but this is something that we will certainly go on working on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Ackerman, do you have any comment to make about that -- these qualifications? Because I -- I think I'm right in thinking that you are the person affected by this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- I think that's probably true. The -- the position of the Pavkovic Defence is -- is not that the 25th May report from General Pavkovic was seen by Ojdanic. It's that we sent it that day. Whether he saw it or not is of no interest to us. If that solves the problem, then we don't have to have a handwriting expert. I'm not sure it does. But we don't make any contention that it was in front of his face, just that we made that report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Their contention is that he never saw it. I don't have any problem with that contention. He probably didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But what's also raised as a possibility is that at some later stage in this case a handwriting expert gives evidence that would have an impact on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, if the purpose of that evidence is to -- to tend to prove that General Ojdanic never saw the document, we agree with that. I'll -- I don't have any contention that he ever saw it. Only that it was sent at the time that it -- that we said it was sent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. So am I reading you correctly as saying that you do not oppose the motion that Mr. Visnjic and Mr. Sepenuk have put to us to qualify the closure of the case in the way indicated?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No. And if they want to bring a handwriting expert, I will probably enjoy cross-examining him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, well. Mr. Stamp, have you any problem with the qualifications to the closure of the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, this is a convenient time to adjourn. The case for the accused Pavkovic will commence on Monday, and my understanding is that it will commence with evidence and without an opening statement, and that will be at 9.00 a.m.?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 9.00 a.m. On Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 22nd day of October, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25
